title: Transistor Fabrication
intro: The front-end steps that build the transistors and the back-end steps that wire them up (Razavi, Section 18.7.1).

items: Start with a p-type wafer, grow a protective oxide, pattern with the n-well mask and implant the wells; strip resist and oxide.

Cover with oxide, nitride and resist and use the active mask so that only the areas between transistors are exposed; implant the channel stop there and grow thick field oxide; strip the nitride and oxide to expose the active areas. (Modern processes use shallow trench isolation instead, see the layout chapter.)

Grow the gate oxide slowly and carefully, then do a threshold-adjust implant: the native thresholds are typically too negative (around 0 V for NMOS and −1 V for PMOS), and a shallow sheet of dopants moves both up.
Deposit polysilicon (it grows on oxide, so it is not crystalline, which does not matter for a conductor), dope it to a few tens of ohms per square, and pattern it with the poly mask.

Implant n+ sources and drains (and n-well ties) with the source/drain mask and a negative resist, then p+ sources and drains (and substrate ties) with the same mask and a positive resist. These implants also dope the poly.

blocks.alt: Cross-section with a p-substrate. On the left an NMOS with n+ source and drain and a poly gate, plus a p+ substrate tie; on the right an n-well containing a PMOS with p+ source and drain and an n+ well tie. Shallow trench oxide separates the regions.
blocks.caption: The result of the front end.

blocks.text: Why the gate comes first: self-alignment

If sources and drains were made before the gate, the gate mask would have to land exactly between them; a misalignment of a fraction of the channel length could leave a gap where no channel forms. Implanting after the gate makes the gate itself the mask: the junctions start precisely at its edges, and a misalignment only makes one junction a little narrower. The earliest CMOS generations did it the other way; self-alignment is what made scaling practical.

items: Silicide: doped poly and diffusion have tens of ohms per square; a thin layer of a metal silicide (titanium silicide, for example) cuts this about tenfold. Oxide spacers on the gate sidewalls keep the silicide on the gate from shorting to the source and drain, so silicidation is self-aligned too (salicide).
Contacts: cover the wafer with 0.3 to 0.5 µm of oxide, pattern with the contact mask and plasma-etch the holes. Contacts to gate poly are not placed over the channel.
Metal 1 (aluminium or copper) is deposited, patterned and etched. Each further layer needs a via mask and a metal mask, so five metals use ten back-end masks.
Passivation: a protective glass over everything, opened only above the bond pads.

blocks.text: Contacts and vias come in one fixed size. A large area is contacted with many small windows rather than one big one, partly because a large aluminium contact can 'spike' down through a shallow junction into the substrate and short it.

blocks.title: Silicide and gate resistance
blocks.text: A gate finger is 2 µm wide and 40 nm long. Find the end-to-end poly resistance with $R_□ = 40\ \Omega/□$ unsilicided and $4\ \Omega/□$ silicided.
solution: The current flows along the 2 µm width over a 40 nm wide strip: 50 squares.

blocks.title: Mask count
blocks.text: Count the masks of a simple process with n-well, active, poly, one source/drain mask (used twice), 5 metal layers (contact or via plus metal for each) and a passivation mask.
solution: Front end: well, active, poly, source/drain = 4.
Total 15 (real processes add threshold, silicide-block, capacitor and other masks).

blocks.title: Misaligned gate
blocks.text: In a self-aligned process the poly mask lands 20 nm to the right of where it was drawn. What happens to the transistor?
solution: The source and drain still start at the actual gate edges, so the channel length and the transistor are unchanged; one junction just gets 20 nm narrower and the other 20 nm wider. Without self-alignment a 20 nm shift could leave an ungated gap and no working device.
blocks.answer: Essentially nothing; one junction is slightly smaller.
